summary: Describes how Ethernet VPN can support Virtual Private Wire Service in MPLS/IP networks. It provides single-active and all-active multihoming with flow-based load balancing, removes the need for pseudowire signaling, and gives fast protection convergence.

plainLanguage.summary: A private cable-like link between two sites over a shared network, with a backup path ready.

subtitle: How Ethernet VPN carries point-to-point wire services over MPLS/IP without pseudowire signaling.

tldr.problem: Point-to-point Ethernet services (VPWS) traditionally rely on pseudowire signaling, which limits redundancy to Single-Active mode and needs two control-plane messages to fail over.
tldr.mechanism: EVPN-VPWS uses one per-EVI Ethernet A-D route per service instance, with the Ethernet Tag ID set to the VPWS service instance identifier, and a new EVPN Layer 2 Attributes extended community with P, B and C flags and an L2 MTU.
tldr.outcome: It provides Single-Active and All-Active multihoming with flow-based load-balancing, removes the need for PW signaling, and converges quickly after a node or link failure.

sections.title: EVPN for Point-to-Point Services
sections.content:
This document describes how EVPN (Ethernet VPN) can support the Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) in MPLS/IP networks. EVPN-VPWS brings the benefits of EVPN to point-to-point (P2P) services: Single-Active redundancy, All-Active redundancy with flow-based load-balancing, and no need for the traditional way of pseudowire (PW) signaling.

It builds on RFC 7432, which can forward customer traffic to or from a given attachment circuit without any MAC lookup, a capability that suits P2P services. The RFC covers two service types: EVPL (Ethernet Virtual Private Line), a P2P service between a pair of attachment circuits designated by VLANs, and EPL (Ethernet Private Line), where all traffic flows between a single pair of ports. In a VPWS service, traffic from one Ethernet Segment can go to only one destination Ethernet Segment, so no MAC lookup is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Many sites use shared networks, but some just want a straight line between two places. This RFC shows how to build that straight line using an existing sharing system and get a backup path too.

sections.title: Service Interfaces
sections.content:
The RFC defines how customer VLANs map to a VPWS service instance identifier. With the VLAN-based interface, one identifier corresponds to a single VLAN on an interface, and if VIDs differ between PEs, frames SHOULD remain tagged with the originating VID and VID translation MUST be done on the disposition PE.

With the VLAN bundle interface, one identifier corresponds to several VLANs on an interface; no VLAN translation is allowed and the MPLS-encapsulated frames MUST remain tagged with the originating VID. The port-based interface is a special case of the bundle where all VLANs on the port map to the same identifier. The VLAN-aware bundle interface is not used in EVPN-VPWS, because it behaves the same as the VLAN-based one.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer can hand over one lane, a group of lanes, or the whole road. The network treats each choice a little differently, but they all end up as one wire between two points.

sections.title: BGP Routes and the Layer 2 Attributes Community
sections.content:
The per-EVI Ethernet A-D route signals the service. Its ESI field is set to the customer Ethernet Segment, and its 32-bit Ethernet Tag ID MUST be set to the VPWS service instance identifier, which MAY be a 24-bit value, right-aligned. Each of the two PEs advertises a route with its own identifier and is configured with the other's identifier; once each has received the other's route, the service instance is instantiated. The Ethernet Tag ID MUST be non-zero for all four service interface types. A given EVPN instance MUST NOT be configured with both VPWS service instances and standard EVPN multipoint services.

The new EVPN Layer 2 Attributes extended community (type 0x06, sub-type 0x04) carries 2 octets of Control Flags, a 2-octet L2 MTU and 2 reserved octets. It is mandatory if multihoming is enabled. The flags are P (the advertising PE is the primary), B (the advertising PE is the backup) and C (a control word MUST be present when sending EVPN packets to this PE). A received non-zero L2 MTU MUST be checked against the local MTU, and on mismatch the local PE MUST NOT add the remote PE as the destination for that service instance; an MTU of zero means no check is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end announces a number for the wire and the other end remembers it. They also swap a small label saying who is primary, who is backup, and how big the packets may be.

sections.title: Operation and Multihoming
sections.content:
All PEs and ASBRs enable the EVPN SAFI and exchange per-EVI Ethernet A-D routes, one route per VPWS service instance. For a single-homed CE, the ESI field is set to zero. For a multihomed CE, the ESI is the CE's ESI and the identifier MUST have the same value on all PEs attached to that segment, which lets an ingress PE in All-Active mode load-balance flows across all of them. The VLAN ID at either end may differ; EVPN does not translate it, the MPLS label identifies the service instance, and any translation is done by the Ethernet interface. Across several ASes, the identifier MUST either be unique across all ASes or an ASBR needs to translate it.

In All-Active mode there is no Designated Forwarder election, and all active PEs set the P flag; remote PEs load-balance per flow among them. In Single-Active mode, the primary PE sets P and clears B, the backup sets B and clears P, and others clear both. If the primary fails, it withdraws its routes and the remote PE sends traffic to the backup. A remote PE MUST receive a P flag from at least one PE before forwarding traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: If a site is plugged into two providers, either both carry traffic or one is boss and one is the spare. Far-away routers know which is which from a flag, and switch to the spare if the boss disappears.

sections.title: Comparison with Pseudowire Signaling and Failure Handling
sections.content:
In EVPN, service endpoint discovery and label signaling happen together using BGP. With VPWS based on RFC 4448, label signaling uses LDP and endpoint discovery is manual or through BGP. Existing PW implementations limit redundancy to Single-Active mode and do not carry traffic on backup PWs, whereas EVPN supports both modes and can load-balance among multihomed PEs.

On failure, EVPN can fail over by withdrawing a single BGP route per service, or one per-ES route for many services, while PW redundancy needs two control-plane messages: one to deactivate the primary group and one to activate the backup group. On a link or port failure, unlike RFC 7432, the PE MUST withdraw all associated Ethernet A-D routes for the VPWS service instances on the failed port, including for single-homed CEs. A per-ES Ethernet A-D route gives mass withdraw. A remote PE MUST NOT use a per-EVI route for forwarding until it has also received the associated per-ES routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way needs two phone calls to switch to the spare line. This way, one announcement saying the main line is gone is enough.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The mechanisms use the EVPN control plane of RFC 7432, so its security considerations apply equally, as do those of the overlay draft cited for the MPLS and IP-based tunnel technologies used for the data plane. The RFC adds no new security text of its own.

IANA allocated EVPN Extended Community sub-type 0x04 for EVPN Layer 2 Attributes and created a registry called EVPN Layer 2 Attributes Control Flags, with RFC Required registration under RFC 8126. The initial entries are P, B and C.
sections.plainLanguage: It reuses the safety rules of the system it builds on and only asks IANA to reserve a new label and a flags list.
